terms.gloss: change one’s mind, change one’s opinion
evidence: Cic. Mur. 61: sententiam mūtāre numquam (Lewis & Short s.v. mūtō)

terms.gloss: change one’s plan, change one’s mind (about what to do)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 4.4.4: ego rogātus mūtāvī cōnsilium meum (Lewis & Short s.v. mūtō)
terms.comment: Sententia is what one thinks, cōnsilium what one means to do: changing one’s mind about going is cōnsilium mūtāre.

evidence: Cic. Prov. Cons. 25: mentēs vestrās voluntātēsque (with mūtāre; Lewis & Short s.v. mūtō)
Traupman 104: to change one’s mind, mentem mūtāre
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase. Cicero uses it of changing people’s disposition and feelings; for a change of opinion or of plan, sententiam or cōnsilium mūtāre is the usual phrase.

terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut.; in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra
evidence: Plaut. Capt. prol. 51: homunculī quantī sunt, quom recōgitō! (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Traupman gives cum ego recōgitō for “on second thought”, literally “when I think it over”. Lewis & Short calls the verb rare: Plautus several times, Cicero once (Q. Fr. 2.2.1).

sources: Lewis & Short: muto · Lewis & Short: sententia · Lewis & Short: consilium
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 104, 289.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
